chapterTitle: Introduction to Web3.js/Ethers.js and the Ethereum Provider

screens.title: Intro to Web3.js, Ethers.js and the Ethereum Provider
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson we open the door from Solidity contracts into usable web applications. You will learn why JavaScript libraries like Web3. js and Ethers. js are essential: they translate browser actions into calls the blockchain understands. We will also define the Provider — the network connection your app uses — and the Signer — the account that can authorize state changes. You will see the common provider types: browser wallets that inject a provider, hosted JSON-RPC services used for read access, and local nodes for development. Practically, we walk through creating a small project, installing Ethers. js, and verifying a read-only connection to a test network. You will also get a safety checklist about A P I keys and private keys so you avoid common security mistakes. By the end you will understand when to use a read-only provider, when to request a signer from a wallet, and how the pieces fit together so your dApp can both show state and submit transactions. Think about which provider fits your next prototype and why.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Introduction
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Introduction to Web3.js / Ethers.js

Connect your frontend to Ethereum using providers and signers so users can read state and submit transactions safely.

Orientation

This chapter explains why you need a JavaScript library, the difference between provider and signer, and how to initialize Ethers.js. You'll practice connecting to a testnet and a local node, and learn common safety practices for keys and API tokens.

Explore Key Topics
Libraries
Why Ethers.js or Web3.js are required to speak the Ethereum protocol from JavaScript.
Providers
Different provider types: browser wallets, JSON-RPC services, and local nodes.
Signers
How signers enable transaction signing while keeping private keys private.
Concept map
Libraries ➜ Provider ➜ Signer ➜ Network
Ethers.js
Modern API, smaller bundle, strong wallet integrations.
Web3.js
Earlier, comprehensive library; concepts transferable.
JSON-RPC
Infura/Alchemy read endpoints used for public queries.
Local Node
Anvil/Ganache for fast development and testing.
Getting started

By installing Ethers and choosing the right provider for your use case, you enable both read-only queries and user-signed transactions. This chapter shows how to do both safely.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this section we make four clear learning goals you can measure. First, you will explain why frontends need a library like Ethers. js or Web3. js. That means being able to describe how a library translates user actions into blockchain requests. Second, you will differentiate an Ethereum provider from a signer, and name common provider types such as browser wallets, hosted JSON-RPC endpoints, and local nodes. Third, you will set up a minimal JavaScript project and install Ethers. js so your workspace is ready. Fourth, you will connect to an Ethereum network using different provider configurations: a browser wallet for signing, an Infura-style JSON-RPC provider for reads, and a local Anvil or Ganache node for development testing. Each objective maps to hands-on checks: describe the role in writing, create a project, run example code, and verify a connection. Treat these as both conceptual and practical milestones: knowing the terms is not enough without the ability to create a working provider connection and to identify when to request a signer. Which of these will you try first?

screens.title: Why frontends need Web3.js or Ethers.js
screens.narratorSegment: A JavaScript library like Ethers. js or Web3. js acts as the translator between your web interface and the Ethereum network. Without such a library, you would manually craft JSON-RPC requests, manage low-level connection details, and handle serialization and deserialization of data. Libraries provide clear abstractions: provider objects to query the network, contract objects to call methods and parse events, and utilities to convert between wei and ether. For example, when a user clicks a button to check a token balance, the library converts that action into a call to the contract's balance function, sends the JSON-RPC request through a provider, and returns a human-friendly value. A common misconception is that libraries are optional; while technically you can call RPC endpoints directly, doing so increases boilerplate and risk and makes wallet integrations harder. The takeaway is pragmatic: use a maintained library to reduce mistakes, handle edge cases, and maintain compatibility with wallets and providers. As a short exercise, inspect a library's contract helper and notice how it simplifies encoding function calls compared to writing raw transaction payloads. Which helper would you depend on first in your next dApp?

keyIdea.title: Library responsibilities
keyIdea.text: Provide provider abstractions, contract helpers, encoding utilities, and safe wallet integrations so the frontend avoids low-level RPC plumbing.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Why libraries?
Definition

A library abstracts JSON-RPC details and offers helpers for providers, contracts, and formatting so your UI can call blockchain functions safely and reliably.

Provider
Handles network connection and JSON-RPC requests.
Contract helper
Encodes and decodes function calls and events for you.
Utilities
Formatting values, unit conversion, and common helpers.
Key Takeaway

Use a maintained library to avoid raw RPC boilerplate and to gain wallet compatibility and safer helpers.

Concrete Example
When a user requests their token balance, the library encodes the balanceOf call, sends it via the provider, and returns a parsed number in ether units. You avoid hand-encoding the ABI and parsing hex responses.
Common Mistake
Attempting to call contracts with handcrafted JSON-RPC payloads increases error surface and makes wallet signing more complex.
Try this
Open a library's contract helper and compare a coded call to a balance function with the manual ABI encoding steps. Notice the simplification.

screens.title: Web3.js versus Ethers.js
screens.narratorSegment: Both Web3. js and Ethers. js allow frontends to interact with Ethereum, but they differ in focus and ergonomics. Web3. js was one of the earliest solutions and offers many features in a single package. Ethers. js emphasizes a smaller bundle, a cleaner A P I, and explicit types of objects such as providers and signers. Concretely, Ethers. js separates concerns: you construct a provider to read state, and you request a signer for transactions. A concrete example: fetching a block number with Ethers requires creating a JsonRpcProvider and calling getBlockNumber, which is concise and predictable. A common misconception is that one library is strictly superior; instead, choose based on project constraints such as bundle size, team familiarity, or needed utilities. For a new dApp where modern wallet flows and compact bundles matter, Ethers. js is a strong default. The final takeaway: the core concepts are transferable, so learning Ethers. js will help you reason about Web3. js code and vice versa. Web3.js versus Ethers.js means ethers.js offers a leaner api and smaller bundles; web3.js is feature-rich. core provider and signer concepts apply to both.. In practical terms, trade-offs: api style, bundle size, and wallet integrations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Library Comparison
Ethers.js — Modern
  • Smaller bundle size and cleaner API.
  • Explicit provider and signer separation.
  • Utilities for formatting and contract interactions.
Example
const provider = new ethers.JsonRpcProvider(SEPOLIA_URL);
const block = await provider.getBlockNumber();
Web3.js — Established
  • Broad functionality and early ecosystem adoption.
  • Different API shape; many projects still rely on it.
  • Concepts overlap: providers, signers, and contracts exist in both.
Misconception
Choosing based solely on popularity can ignore bundle and security implications. Match the library to your app needs.
Key Takeaway

Ethers.js is often preferred for modern dApps for its clarity and compactness, but both libraries teach the same provider and signer model.

screens.title: What is a Provider?
screens.narratorSegment: A Provider is the abstraction your application uses to talk to an Ethereum node. It hides networking details and exposes methods to query chain state, fetch blocks, and send raw transactions when combined with a signer. Think of a provider as a read-and-relay service: it accepts high-level requests like getting a block number or reading a contract method and returns parsed results. There are three common types: browser-injected providers from wallets, hosted JSON-RPC services like Infura, and local development nodes such as Anvil or Ganache. A concrete example is creating a JsonRpcProvider with a URL and calling getBalance to retrieve an address balance. A common confusion is expecting a provider to sign transactions; it cannot sign without a signer. The provider is about connectivity and data; separate signer objects add signature capability. The final practical point: choose the provider type based on whether you need public read access, user signing, or fast local iteration. What is a Provider? means providers give your app access to blockchain data and relay requests; signing requires a separate signer object or wallet.. In practical terms, the application's network connection to ethereum. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Provider
Provider role

Provides network access, JSON-RPC relay, and methods to read chain state such as balances, blocks, and logs.

Example call
const provider = new ethers.JsonRpcProvider(URL); const block = await provider.getBlockNumber();
Not a signer
A provider alone cannot sign transactions; use a signer for state changes.
Provider types
Browser-based
Injected by wallets like MetaMask for user accounts and signing requests.
JSON-RPC services
Infura or Alchemy provide hosted endpoints for read-heavy operations.
Local nodes
Anvil or Ganache for fast development and deterministic accounts.
Key Takeaway

Pick the provider type that matches your read and signing needs: wallet for user signing, hosted for public reads, local for testing.

screens.title: Browser-based Providers (MetaMask)
screens.narratorSegment: Browser wallets inject a provider into the web page so dApps can request access to user accounts. The typical flow is: detect the injected provider, request account access, obtain a signer or account address, then use that signer to send transactions. For example, your app checks for window. ethereum and then asks the wallet to enable accounts. Upon user approval, the wallet exposes the signer that can sign messages and transactions while keeping the private key secure inside the extension. A common mistake is assuming user accounts are available without requesting permission; modern wallets require explicit consent. Another pitfall is trying to read private key material from the page — wallets never expose keys. Practice the flow by requesting accounts and then attempting a read-only call with the obtained provider before sending a signed transaction. The takeaway: always request permission, obtain a signer for transactions, and trust the wallet to handle signing securely. Browser-based Providers (MetaMask) means detect the injected provider, request account access, then request a signer for transactions while the wallet holds keys securely.. In practical terms, detecting and requesting a signer from an injected provider. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Browser Wallets
Step-by-step
  1. Detect injected provider (e.g., window.ethereum).
  2. Request account access from the user.
  3. Get a signer from the provider for transaction signing.
  4. Use signer to send transactions; provider for reads.
Concrete Tips
Always ask for permission; wallets will prompt the user to approve account access.
Do not attempt to access private keys. Use the signer object provided by the wallet to sign requests.
Handle network changes: the user may be on a different chain than your app expects.
Check your understanding

Can you describe why a site must request permission to access accounts and what a signer allows the dApp to do that a provider alone cannot?

screens.title: JSON-RPC Providers (Infura, Alchemy)
screens.narratorSegment: JSON-RPC providers like Infura or Alchemy run node infrastructure and expose endpoints your application can call to fetch blockchain data. These services are convenient for read-heavy operations, analytics dashboards, or backend tasks that don't require a user-signed transaction. For instance, a web app showing recent transfers could query a hosted endpoint for logs and display results without prompting users to connect a wallet. To use such a provider, you typically create a JsonRpcProvider with the service URL or project ID. A concrete example is connecting to the Sepolia testnet via an Infura project ID and calling getBlockNumber to verify connectivity. A common mistake is embedding secret keys intended for write operations directly in frontend code; read-only project IDs are often safe but treat tokens carefully. The practical guideline is to use hosted providers for public reads and as fallbacks, while relying on wallet signers for user-authenticated writes. JSON-RPC Providers (Infura, Alchemy) means use infura or alchemy for reliable read access and backend services; avoid exposing secret write credentials in client code.. In practical terms, hosted nodes for public reads and backend services. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › JSON-RPC Providers
How they fit

Hosted JSON-RPC providers act as remote nodes you can query for blockchain data. They are ideal for public reads and backend services that do not require user signatures.

Example code
import { ethers } from 'ethers';
const sepoliaUrl = `https://sepolia.infura.io/v3/YOUR_PROJECT_ID`;
const provider = new ethers.JsonRpcProvider(sepoliaUrl);
const blockNumber = await provider.getBlockNumber();
Practical notes
Use read-only project IDs in public frontends when possible and avoid exposing write secrets.
Hosted providers are useful as fallbacks when a user has no wallet connected.
Rate limits may apply; design caching and backends accordingly.
Key Takeaway

Hosted providers are reliable for reads and server tasks; keep sensitive credentials off the client and prefer backends for write operations.

screens.title: Local Providers: Anvil and Ganache
screens.narratorSegment: Local development nodes like Anvil or Ganache let you iterate quickly without relying on public networks. They provide deterministic accounts, immediate mining, and a JSON-RPC endpoint typically at http://127.0.0.1:8545. The common workflow is to start the node, inspect the pre-funded accounts it provides, and point your provider to the local RPC URL. For example, you can run Anvil, create a JsonRpcProvider at the local address, fetch the block number, list accounts, and read balances. A practical benefit is you can test transactions instantly without waiting for a testnet. A misconception is thinking local providers behave exactly like public networks; they are often more permissive and should not be used as a security proxy. Use them for testing logic and UI flows, then validate behavior on a testnet before production. The key is speed: local nodes remove network latency and allow deterministic testing of contract interactions. Local Providers: Anvil and Ganache means use anvil or ganache for fast, deterministic testing with immediate transaction finality and accessible test accounts.. In practical terms, fast development and deterministic accounts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Local Providers
Start and connect
  1. Run Anvil or Ganache locally.
  2. Create an ethers.JsonRpcProvider pointing at http://127.0.0.1:8545.
  3. List accounts and read balances to verify.
Example verification
After connecting, call getBlockNumber and listAccounts to confirm the node is running and accounts are available for testing.
Tip
Use local nodes for automated tests and UI flows. Always re-test on a public testnet before release.

screens.title: Set up a basic project and install Ethers.js
screens.narratorSegment: Setting up a minimal project is straightforward and gives you a safe place to experiment. Start by creating a folder, running npm init -y to create a package manifest, and then npm install ethers to add Ethers. js. This creates a node_modules folder and updates package. json with the dependency. Next, create a JavaScript file such as index. js that imports Ethers and constructs a provider. For example, import { ethers } from 'ethers' and then create a JsonRpcProvider with an endpoint. A concrete example is connecting to Sepolia with an Infura URL. Remember to store any A P I project IDs in environment variables or a backend when used for sensitive write operations. A misconception is committing node_modules or secret files to source control; instead, add node_modules and. env to. gitignore and keep secrets out of the repository. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Sepolia Example
Starter script
import { ethers } from 'ethers';
const INFURA_PROJECT_ID = 'YOUR_INFURA_PROJECT_ID';
const sepoliaUrl = `https://sepolia.infura.io/v3/${INFURA_PROJECT_ID}`;
async function main(){
  const provider = new ethers.JsonRpcProvider(sepoliaUrl);
  const blockNumber = await provider.getBlockNumber();
  console.log('Connected. Block:', blockNumber);
}
main();
Run node index.js and confirm a printed block number. If you see errors, check your project ID and network status.

screens.title: Signer: who can sign transactions?
screens.narratorSegment: A signer is an object that can cryptographically sign messages and transactions using an account's private key. In practice, signers are provided by wallets such as MetaMask or created from a private key on a backend. The difference from a provider is important: a provider can read blockchain state and relay requests, but it cannot sign on behalf of an account. For example, to send ETH or call a contract method that changes state, you need a signer to produce a signed transaction. A common error is attempting to send a transaction with only a provider. Another pitfall is exposing a raw private key in client-side code; never do this. Instead, request a signer from a wallet or delegate signing to a secure backend. A practical exercise is to request a signer from MetaMask, prepare a simple transaction, and observe that the wallet prompts the user to confirm, ensuring the private key never leaves the wallet. This contrast clarifies why providers and signers together enable both reading and writing safely. Starter code
import { ethers } from 'ethers';
async function connectToLocalNetwork(){
  const provider = new ethers.JsonRpcProvider('http://127.0.0.1:8545');
  const blockNumber = await provider.getBlockNumber();
  const accounts = await provider.listAccounts();
  // if accounts[0] has an address property:
  const first = accounts[0]?.address || accounts[0];
  const balance = await provider.getBalance(first);
  console.log(blockNumber, first, ethers.formatEther(balance));
}
connectToLocalNetwork();
Run this with node after ensuring Anvil or Ganache is running. You should see a block number and a balance printed.

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this lesson we open the door from Solidity contracts into usable web applications. You will learn why JavaScript libraries like Web3. js and Ethers. js are essential: they translate browser actions into calls the blockchain understands. We will also define the Provider — the network connection your app uses — and the Signer — the account that can authorize state changes. You will see the common provider types: browser wallets that inject a provider, hosted JSON-RPC services used for read access, and local nodes for development. Practically, we walk through creating a small project, installing Ethers. js, and verifying a read-only connection to a test network. You will also get a safety checklist about A P I keys and private keys so you avoid common security mistakes. By the end you will understand when to use a read-only provider, when to request a signer from a wallet, and how the pieces fit together so your dApp can both show state and submit transactions. Think about which provider fits your next prototype and why.

In this section we make four clear learning goals you can measure. First, you will explain why frontends need a library like Ethers. js or Web3. js. That means being able to describe how a library translates user actions into blockchain requests. Second, you will differentiate an Ethereum provider from a signer, and name common provider types such as browser wallets, hosted JSON-RPC endpoints, and local nodes. Third, you will set up a minimal JavaScript project and install Ethers. js so your workspace is ready. Fourth, you will connect to an Ethereum network using different provider configurations: a browser wallet for signing, an Infura-style JSON-RPC provider for reads, and a local Anvil or Ganache node for development testing. Each objective maps to hands-on checks: describe the role in writing, create a project, run example code, and verify a connection. Treat these as both conceptual and practical milestones: knowing the terms is not enough without the ability to create a working provider connection and to identify when to request a signer. Which of these will you try first?

Now let's connect those objectives to specific actions you will perform. For explaining libraries, you will write a short note describing how Ethers. js exposes provider and contract abstractions. For differentiating provider and signer, you will identify which operations require a signer — typically sending a transaction — and which only need a provider for reading state. For installing Ethers. js, you will run npm init and npm install so you can import Ethers in a project file. For connecting, you will run example code that queries the current block number from Sepolia, and you will run a local script against Anvil or Ganache to read the first account's balance. Each practice task is small, fast, and verifiable; together they ensure you not only know the definitions but can run a provider, request a signer, and observe blockchain responses. Finally, treat A P I keys and private keys carefully: use environment variables and never embed private keys in client-side code.

A JavaScript library like Ethers. js or Web3. js acts as the translator between your web interface and the Ethereum network. Without such a library, you would manually craft JSON-RPC requests, manage low-level connection details, and handle serialization and deserialization of data. Libraries provide clear abstractions: provider objects to query the network, contract objects to call methods and parse events, and utilities to convert between wei and ether. For example, when a user clicks a button to check a token balance, the library converts that action into a call to the contract's balance function, sends the JSON-RPC request through a provider, and returns a human-friendly value. A common misconception is that libraries are optional; while technically you can call RPC endpoints directly, doing so increases boilerplate and risk and makes wallet integrations harder. The takeaway is pragmatic: use a maintained library to reduce mistakes, handle edge cases, and maintain compatibility with wallets and providers. As a short exercise, inspect a library's contract helper and notice how it simplifies encoding function calls compared to writing raw transaction payloads. Which helper would you depend on first in your next dApp?

Both Web3. js and Ethers. js allow frontends to interact with Ethereum, but they differ in focus and ergonomics. Web3. js was one of the earliest solutions and offers many features in a single package. Ethers. js emphasizes a smaller bundle, a cleaner A P I, and explicit types of objects such as providers and signers. Concretely, Ethers. js separates concerns: you construct a provider to read state, and you request a signer for transactions. A concrete example: fetching a block number with Ethers requires creating a JsonRpcProvider and calling getBlockNumber, which is concise and predictable. A common misconception is that one library is strictly superior; instead, choose based on project constraints such as bundle size, team familiarity, or needed utilities. For a new dApp where modern wallet flows and compact bundles matter, Ethers. js is a strong default. The final takeaway: the core concepts are transferable, so learning Ethers. js will help you reason about Web3. js code and vice versa. A Provider is the abstraction your application uses to talk to an Ethereum node. It hides networking details and exposes methods to query chain state, fetch blocks, and send raw transactions when combined with a signer. Think of a provider as a read-and-relay service: it accepts high-level requests like getting a block number or reading a contract method and returns parsed results. There are three common types: browser-injected providers from wallets, hosted JSON-RPC services like Infura, and local development nodes such as Anvil or Ganache. A concrete example is creating a JsonRpcProvider with a URL and calling getBalance to retrieve an address balance. A common confusion is expecting a provider to sign transactions; it cannot sign without a signer. The provider is about connectivity and data; separate signer objects add signature capability. Browser wallets inject a provider into the web page so dApps can request access to user accounts. A signer is an object that can cryptographically sign messages and transactions using an account's private key. In practice, signers are provided by wallets such as MetaMask or created from a private key on a backend. The difference from a provider is important: a provider can read blockchain state and relay requests, but it cannot sign on behalf of an account. For example, to send ETH or call a contract method that changes state, you need a signer to produce a signed transaction. A common error is attempting to send a transaction with only a provider. Another pitfall is exposing a raw private key in client-side code; never do this. Instead, request a signer from a wallet or delegate signing to a secure backend. A practical exercise is to request a signer from MetaMask, prepare a simple transaction, and observe that the wallet prompts the user to confirm, ensuring the private key never leaves the wallet. This contrast clarifies why providers and signers together enable both reading and writing safely. Let's consolidate the essentials. First: libraries such as Ethers. js and Web3. js are the bridge that translates frontend actions into blockchain requests and provide helpers for contract calls and formatting. Second: a Provider connects your application to a node for reads and relaying requests, while a Signer is required to sign and send state-changing transactions; wallets provide signers securely. Third: choose the right provider for the job — browser wallets for user-signed transactions, hosted JSON-RPC services for read-heavy frontends or backends, and local nodes for fast, deterministic development. Keep A P I keys and private keys protected: never embed sensitive write credentials in client code. These concepts combined let you design a frontend that reads state safely and prompts users for signing only when necessary. This quick reference reinforces three short definitions. A Provider is your app's network access point for reading blockchain data and relaying requests. A Signer is an account-capable object that can sign transactions and messages, typically provided by a wallet and never exposing private keys to the page. And Ethers. js or Web3. js are the JavaScript libraries that package these abstractions with contract helpers and utility functions. Keep these concise definitions in mind as you set up projects and debug connections: if you cannot fetch a block, check the provider; if you cannot send a transaction, check the signer and wallet permissions; if your code feels verbose for contract calls, inspect library helpers for simpler patterns.
